newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Pork crisis rocks Taiwan, seen curbing GDP growth.
newsitem.headline: Pork crisis rocks Taiwan, seen curbing GDP growth.

text.p: Taiwan faces one of its biggest economic crises in years with lucrative pork exports brought to a halt from March 20 due to an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease among its large number of hogs.
Breeders fearful of huge income losses on Sunday threatened to set free hundreds of diseased pigs in Taipei to protest what they viewed as the government's failure to control the disease.

"If the government fails to give us reasonable subsidies and offer us financial and technical aid to slaughter the diseased pigs, we will not rule out setting free hundreds of pigs in Taipei," an official with the Hog Breeding Association told Reuters.
He said a meeting of breeders on Friday decided the government needs to provide T$3,000 (US$109) per kg in compensation for each pig slaughtered.
The government's Council of Agriculture (COA) has agreed to provide T$2,400 (US$87.2) per kg for each meat hog slaughtered.
COA figures showed that 37,569 pigs in 5,919 breeding farms in 12 counties were found to have contracted the deadly and contagious disease, while 11,943 had died of it as of March 22.
Breeders estimated the number of infected hogs at more than 150,000, out of total hog population of 14 million.
Usually fatal in livestock, the disease is rarely contracted by humans, although they can be carriers of it.
Taiwan television aired footage of breeders complaining of government inaction and bursting into tears as health officials electrocuted pigs suspected of being infected.
Local newspapers reported that some veterinarians had warned agriculture and health authorities of a possible outbreak of the disease a year ago but the government failed to act.
Chiu Mao-ying, chairman of the COA, said on state television on Sunday that the government was doing all it could to curb the disease's spread.
The outbreak has resulted in a halt to pork product output by leading food processing companies.
But perhaps hardest hit were pork exporters as major importers like Japan and South Korea banned Taiwan pork.
Taiwan pork exports totalled US$1.55 billion in 1996, according to the Board of Foreign Trade.

Chan Teh-sung, a bureau director in the government's Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, said on Saturday the lost exports would cut Taiwan's total gross domestic product (GDP) forecast for 1997 by 0.5 of a percentage point to 5.78 percent.
The economics ministry said if all 14 million hogs became infected the GDP growth rate would be cut by a further 1.4 percent.
Government statistics show the export ban may cost as many as 50,000 jobs, which will add some 0.5-0.6 of a percentage point to the island's jobless rate.
But Chien Chin-ching, chairman of the Taiwan Agriculture Association, said about one million people are involved in pork-related work.
"It is necessary for the government to help these people change jobs," he said.
